levels.25.title: A bonus photon
levels.25.intro: When two electrons collide, sometimes an extra photon flies out: braking radiation. Two vertices are no longer enough.
levels.25.steps.build.prompt: Build e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ using all three vertices: the electrons exchange a photon and the top one then emits a real photon.
levels.25.steps.build.hints.0: Follow electron 1's line: it comes in, interacts, emits and goes out. Each stop is a vertex.
levels.25.steps.build.hints.1: Top: 1 → left vertex → right vertex → 3. The right vertex emits the real photon; the left one exchanges a photon with electron 2.
levels.25.steps.order.prompt: This process has one more vertex than Møller scattering. How does its probability change?
levels.25.steps.order.options.same.feedb: Each vertex adds a factor e to the amplitude: it can't be the same.
levels.25.steps.order.options.alpha.text: It's about 137 times less likely (a factor α)
levels.25.steps.order.options.alpha.feed: The amplitude gains a factor e; the probability, e², that is, α ≈ 1/137.
levels.25.steps.order.options.more.text: It's more likely, because there are more particles
levels.25.steps.order.options.more.feedb: More vertices means more factors of e, and e is small.
levels.25.steps.order.hints.0: Amplitude ∝ eⁿ, with n the number of vertices.
levels.25.steps.order.hints.1: The probability is |𝓜|²: each extra vertex multiplies it by e², which is proportional to α.
levels.25.success: You've built your first three-vertex diagram: a process with radiation.
levels.25.explanation.intuitive: A charge that suddenly changes direction emits light. Here, the light comes out of the electron that has just been pushed.
levels.25.explanation.scientific: It's braking radiation (bremsstrahlung) in Møller scattering. It's a process of order e³ in the amplitude: it's suppressed by a factor α compared with scattering without a photon, but it dominates the energy loss of fast electrons in matter.
levels.25.explanation.math: 𝓜 ∝ e³. dσ(ee → eeγ) ∼ α · dσ(ee → ee) · (emission factor), with dσ ∝ α³ overall.
levels.26.title: How many stories?
levels.26.intro: With three vertices, the extra photon can come out of many places. Before calculating, a physicist counts all the possible stories.
levels.26.steps.when.prompt: Play the diagram in time. When is the real photon emitted?
levels.26.steps.when.options.before.feed: Look at the order of the vertices: the real photon comes out of the last one.
levels.26.steps.when.options.never.text: There's no real photon, only the virtual one
levels.26.steps.when.options.never.feedb: The wavy line ending at the right edge is a real outgoing photon.
levels.26.steps.when.hints.0: Press ▶ and watch which vertex lights up last.
levels.26.steps.when.hints.1: The right vertex, which emits the real photon, is the last one in time.
levels.26.steps.where.prompt: In this other story, tap the vertex where the real photon is born.
levels.26.steps.where.wrong.vA: That vertex emits the virtual photon the electrons exchange.
levels.26.steps.where.wrong.vB: That vertex absorbs the virtual photon.
levels.26.steps.where.wrongDefault: Look for a vertex: the points on the edges are external particles.
levels.26.steps.where.hints.0: Follow the wavy line that ends at the edge.
levels.26.steps.where.hints.1: It's on electron 2's line, before the exchange.
levels.26.steps.where.solved: Here electron 2 radiates before interacting. It's another contribution to the same process.
levels.26.steps.count.prompt: The real photon can come out of any of the 4 electron lines, and there are 2 ways to pair up the electrons (t and u). How many tree-level diagrams does e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ have?
levels.26.steps.count.options.4.feedback: That only counts one pairing. Remember the t and u channels.
levels.26.steps.count.options.8.feedback: 4 lines to attach the photon to × 2 channels = 8 stories.
levels.26.steps.count.options.16.feedbac: The photon can't come out of the virtual line: a photon has no charge and doesn't emit another photon.
levels.26.success: Counting the stories correctly is the first step of any real calculation.
levels.26.explanation.intuitive: Each place where the photon can be born is a different story. Nature goes through all of them at once.
levels.26.explanation.scientific: There are 8 tree-level diagrams for e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ: the photon attaches to any of the 4 external electron lines, in the t and u channels. The 8 amplitudes are added (with Pauli's relative sign between t and u) before squaring.
levels.26.explanation.math: 𝓜 = Σᵢ 𝓜ᵢ, with 8 terms ∝ e³. The game checks this by enumerating every trivalent tree with 5 leaves that satisfies the vertex rule.
levels.27.title: Three flashes
levels.27.intro: Positronium is a short-lived atom: an electron and a positron orbiting each other. One of its forms dies by emitting three photons.
levels.27.steps.build.prompt: Build e⁻e⁺ → γγγ. A single fermion line runs through all three vertices and each vertex emits a photon.
levels.27.steps.build.hints.0: The arrow comes in with the electron, passes through all three vertices and goes out toward the positron.
levels.27.steps.build.hints.1: Electron → top vertex → middle vertex → bottom vertex → positron (arrow toward the positron). One photon at each vertex.
levels.27.steps.count.prompt: The three photons are identical. How many different diagrams are there, changing which photon comes out of each vertex?
levels.27.steps.count.options.1.feedback: Try swapping two photons: it connects the same particles differently.
levels.27.steps.count.options.6.feedback: 3 · 2 · 1 = 6 ways to share three photons among three vertices.
levels.27.steps.count.hints.0: The first vertex can emit any of the 3 photons; the second, either of the 2 left.
levels.27.success: You've drawn the decay of ortho-positronium.
levels.27.explanation.intuitive: Matter and antimatter meet and turn into three flashes of light.
levels.27.explanation.scientific: Positronium with parallel spins (ortho-positronium) can't decay into two photons: charge-conjugation symmetry forbids it. That's why it emits three, lives about a thousand times longer than para-positronium (which emits two), and its decay rate is a precision test of QED.
levels.27.explanation.math: 6 diagrams, each ∝ e³. Γ(o-Ps → 3γ) ∝ α⁶ mₑ, versus Γ(p-Ps → 2γ) ∝ α⁵ mₑ.
levels.28.title: Permutations
levels.28.intro: Identical photons don't have names of their own. Swapping them gives another story that also counts.
levels.28.steps.other.prompt: Build a contribution to e⁻e⁺ → γγγ different from the reference one.
levels.28.steps.other.reference.label: Reference
levels.28.steps.other.hints.0: The electron line is already there. You only have to decide which photon comes out of each vertex.
levels.28.steps.other.hints.1: Swap two photons compared with the reference: for example, 1 from the middle vertex and 2 from the top one.
levels.28.steps.sign.prompt: In Møller, the two diagrams were subtracted. How do these six contributions with identical photons combine?
levels.28.steps.sign.options.plus.text: They all add with the same sign
levels.28.steps.sign.options.plus.feedba: Photons are bosons: swapping them doesn't change the sign of the amplitude.
levels.28.steps.sign.options.minus.text: The signs alternate, as in Møller
levels.28.steps.sign.options.minus.feedb: The minus sign appears when swapping identical fermions, not bosons.
levels.28.steps.sign.options.one.text: Only one counts, because the photons are the same
levels.28.steps.sign.options.one.feedbac: Precisely because they're indistinguishable, every story contributes.
levels.28.steps.sign.hints.1: Pauli's minus sign only appears with identical fermions.
levels.28.success: You can now tell how identical bosons and fermions combine.
levels.28.explanation.intuitive: Swapping two identical photons gives a new story, just as valid, that adds to the others.
levels.28.explanation.scientific: For identical bosons the amplitude is symmetric under exchange: the 6 permutations add with a + sign. For identical fermions it's antisymmetric (Møller's − sign). This difference explains Bose–Einstein statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle.
levels.28.explanation.math: 𝓜 = Σ_{σ ∈ S₃} 𝓜(k_σ(1), k_σ(2), k_σ(3)), with a + sign for every term.
